stories.title: The Internet goes on high alert after discovery of 8 compromised TLS certs
stories.summary: Heartbleed is the name of a critical vulnerability in the OpenSSL cryptography library. In 2014, it came under mass exploitation. Exploits let many unaffiliated hackers decrypt TLS-protected exchanges between parties. They also recovered private TLS certificate keys, session cookies, and passwords. The attacks compromised thousands of servers, some belonging to large companies and government agencies around the world. Recovery required a long series of steps that took years. Steps included patching OpenSSL on all affected devices, reissuing millions of TLS keys, revoking old certificates, rotating passwords and session tokens and updating embedded devices and other forgotten systems—something that was extremely time- and resource-intensive, especially at Internet scale.

stories.title: UNC-Chapel Hill strikes bargain with Trump administration to end probes
stories.summary: The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill on Monday struck a deal with the Trump administration to end federal investigations into its handling of alleged campus antisemitism and civil rights violations. Under the terms, the highly selective public flagship will share with the federal government years’ worth data on civil rights complaints and adopt new policies, ranging from admissions changes to student activity oversight. In exchange, the U.S. departments of Justice and Education will end more than a dozen active civil rights probes into the university. UNC-Chapel Hill did not admit wrongdoing under the agreement, and the federal government said it does not intend to dictate the "content of academic speech or curricula" at the university.

It’s great,” he said, adding that the US move would save lives. So we are thankful to the American side.” Witkoff will on Wednesday meet Russian president Vladimir Putin after what a US official called “constructive” talks with Zelenskyy in Norway.

reserveStories.summary: A hacker broke into more than 100 websites using an army of AI agents that mostly operated on their own, according to findings from the AI security firm Norforge. Though Norforge doesn’t name the targets, Reuters reports that the victims included companies like John Deere, SharkNinja, and Cummins. Concerns over AI-powered cybersecurity breaches have grown as the technology grows more advanced, with hackers using the tools to carry out large-scale attacks. At the same time, rogue AI agents are carrying out attacks of their own after escaping from testing environments. Researchers at Norforge uncovered the attacks through exposed work on Cairn, an open-source AI platform that describes itself as a “general-purpose problem-solving engine.”
